3.text: easy ways of the Russian creoles of the Kolyma in love affairs make Russian

4.text: girls quite accessible to the young Chukchee men through some small present,

6.text: Still, the difference between the life of Russian fishermen living in warm

7.text: block-houses within the forest border, and that of the Chukchee reindeer-

8.text: breeders living on the treeless tundra in cold and open tents, is very great.

9.text: So in the winter-time the Russian women, clad in the shaggy clothes of the

10.text: Chukchee woman’s dress, are helpless enough to look upon; nor are they

11.text: very good workers and housewives, in the Chukchee sense of the word; not

12.text: one of them is capable of beating the hoary cover of the sleeping-room with

13.text: sufficient force and perseverance. The work of a Russian woman in the

14.text: Kolyma country is incomparably easier than that of the wife of a Chukchee.

15.text: Russian relatives and neighbors make fun of women given to savages, be-

16.text: cause such marriages are considered humiliating. Perhaps to keep off jeers,

17.text: all these women enter with great energy upon their new life, and talk with

18.text: some disdain of their former life on the river. I remember one whom I

19.text: visited in mid-winter. It was bitter cold; and since she had been staying in

20.text: the open since early morning, and was clad in the strange loose combination-

21.text: suit of Chukchee cut, with half-bare neck and shoulders, her face was blue,

22.text: and her fingers stiff, and she was able to keep some warmth in her body

23.text: only by constant movement and work. Still she praised that life. “There

24.text: on the river the people are hungry,” she explained, “but our food walks

25.text: around us on its four legs.” Nevertheless these women have confessed that

26.text: the first months of their life on the tundra were very hard. “One knows

27.text: neither the language nor the ways of life. One feels a yearning to go back

28.text: to the river, and weeps all the time. Then comes an old ‘knowing woman’

29.text: and performs an incantation, which takes away the sorrow and makes one

30.text: more adapted to the new life.”

31.text: The Russian women on the river said about this, that the Chukchee

32.text: witches, with their incantations, take out of the woman the Russian soul and

33.text: put in its place a Chukchee soul. Therefore these women ever afterwards

34.text: love life in the open. I must mention that I know of hardly one case where

35.text: a woman like that would return from the savage tundra to the civilized “river.”

36.text: Indeed, one of the women told me that after the death of her first Chukchee

37.text: husband, she came back to her native village, having with her a small son

38.text: of three years. “But we could not live there for too long a time,” she said,

39.text: on account of the stifled air of the block-house. We got violent headaches.

40.text: Food was scarce, only dried fish; but the boy was not accustomed to it, and

41.text: asked for reindeer-meat. At last, after staying three months in the village,

42.text: I married another Chukchee, and went with him to the tundra again.”
